title: AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production
gist: An InfoQ Live panel (Garima Bajpai, Martin Reynolds of Harness, Patrick Debois, Gunnar Grosch of Sinch, moderated by Renato Losio) argues AI has made code abundant but shifted the bottleneck to review, testing, security and governance downstream of code generation. The consensus answer is risk-tiered automation, least-privilege scoped credentials and auditability for agents, small changes, and outcome-driven ROI rather than FOMO-driven tooling.

themes.theme: From solo coding agents to the software factory

insights.claim: Tessl adviser Patrick Debois describes a staged AI adoption path — autocomplete, then laptop coding agents, then shared context/skills, then (about six to seven months ago at his company) a central 'factory' pipeline where tickets are filed and agents execute them, pulling product, engineering, sales and support into one workflow.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Vendors selling centralized agent pipelines/orchestration (vs. per-developer seats) map to the next adoption stage; watch for spend shifting from IDE assistants to factory platforms.
insights.quote: About six or seven months ago, we switched to using a central pipeline, what we call the factory in general, where we're all working more through filing tickets, the agents take care of it
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: We're probably going through these phases

insights.claim: Sinch developer advocate Gunnar Grosch observes that teams readily hand off the research phase and the deploy/test/iterate loop to agents, but the core implementation step in between still remains with human engineers, largely because of trust.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: The 'middle' of the lifecycle is the unconquered TAM for agent vendors; trust/verification tooling is the unlock.
insights.quote: I think a lot of it comes down to trust, being able to actually hand off that entire work. It's a bit scary.
insights.locator: What I'm still seeing a lot is

insights.claim: InfoQ editor Renato Losio reports that most practitioners he talks to are experimenting with agent-driven delivery, but few run it fully in production with trust — it remains mostly proofs of concept or small projects.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Production adoption of autonomous delivery lags the hype; revenue expectations for agentic DevOps vendors should be tempered near term.
insights.locator: Agentic Software Delivery, in Prod

insights.claim: Gunnar Grosch argues most organizations need not emulate Anthropic's fully automated agents (cited as pushing on the order of 30,000 PRs per day), drawing an analogy to how not every company needed Netflix-style chaos engineering in production.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: Expect a long tail of partially automated adopters rather than wholesale autonomy; tooling that supports gradual autonomy fits the market better.
insights.quote: Not everyone is Anthropic and has to have fully automated agents that are pushing 30,000 PRs per day or whatever that number is.
insights.locator: Gunnar Grosch: I think it's funny

themes.theme: Risk-tiered review and the human bottleneck

insights.claim: Patrick Debois frames AI change governance as likelihood (better context and tests reduce issues), risk analysis (a docs change differs from an authentication change) and production impact (architect around failure), arguing teams over-optimize output and under-think risk tolerance.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Risk-scoring and blast-radius tooling becomes a core control point in AI delivery pipelines.
insights.quote: A lot of people just focus on optimizing the results, but they don't think about risk.
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: I love that you're bringing up the compliance

insights.claim: Harness Field CTO Martin Reynolds says human review is now the status quo bottleneck across PRs, test writing and security triage because delivery systems were designed for human-speed code generation while AI has accelerated only the front of the pipeline.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Spend and product opportunity is shifting 'right' of code generation — CI/CD, review, security remediation (Harness's own pitch).
insights.quote: Most of these systems were designed for changes that happened at human writing code speeds.
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: That's pretty much the status quo

insights.claim: Harness takes a risk-based approach where low-risk PRs may be accepted by AI without a human, with risk scored on metrics such as code stability, rework history and the outcome of the last 10 deployments, and it uses a different AI for reviewing than for coding.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Separation of generator and reviewer models is emerging as a governance norm — supports multi-model/multi-vendor demand.
insights.quote: We don't use the same AI for coding that we use for reviewing, just like you wouldn't use the same person to review.
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: I know internally

insights.claim: Gunnar Grosch argues that if PR volume doubles without doubling reviewers, review must change — but simply automating review with AI is not the answer; prioritizing deep review by risk is.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: Skepticism of pure 'AI reviews AI' products; differentiation will come from risk triage rather than blanket automated approval.
insights.quote: The solution isn't to automate it with AI either, because reviewing AI, is not the answer to the question.
insights.locator: Gunnar Grosch: It is simple math

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds remains a strong advocate of small changes because humans are poor at reviewing thousand-line diffs, and AI can help by isolating the functionally meaningful portion of a large diff (e.g. separating dependency-version churn from real logic changes).
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Diff-summarization and change-focus features are practical value-adds for review tools.
insights.quote: When you get a diff with a thousand lines, humans are rubbish at reading a thousand-line changes.
insights.locator: Here's the bit that actually changed in the functional

insights.claim: Patrick Debois highlights a review gap: two PRs can each be correct and mergeable yet semantically incompatible (e.g. one changes an invoice total function to cents while another builds a report assuming dollars), and current reviews do not check compatibility of intent.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Intent-level/semantic conflict detection is an unaddressed tooling niche as agent PR volume grows.
insights.quote: they are mergeable, they are correct, but they're both semantically incompatible
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: I want to give one example

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai says her teams have started measuring 'intent to production' metrics and predicts intent itself will soon become the backlog and bottleneck as code production becomes abundant.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Engineering productivity metrics (DORA-style) may shift toward intent-to-production; product/requirements capacity becomes the constraint.
insights.quote: This is my personal belief that in no time, intent will become the backlog and bottleneck.
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: I think this is an excellent point

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds cites Anthropic's Claude Code paper as reporting roughly six hours of agent time per human hour, with agents idle about 80% of the time waiting for human approvals — and warns humans are very good at rubber-stamping approvals.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Approval UX and policy-based auto-approval are the throughput lever; idle agent time is wasted compute/spend.
insights.quote: humans are very good at saying yes
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: There was another piece to that thing

insights.claim: Patrick Debois mentions an experiment that found the acceptance rate for AI-written code rose on weekends, suggesting human approval quality degrades with context and attention.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop controls are weaker than assumed; supports demand for deterministic policy gates.
insights.quote: the acceptance rate for AI written code went up in the weekend
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: There was somewhere an experiment

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai argues testing must shift for probabilistic LLM applications from statistical thresholds to golden data points and LLM-as-judge rubrics, and that security must shift right to runtime rather than only shift left.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Runtime security and LLM evaluation tooling are growth categories in AI-era DevSecOps.
insights.quote: Security must transition to runtime.
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: I actually wanted to add a few things

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds notes the most effective AI users are generally senior developers, and that because AI-generated code produces more issues, more live incidents and more CVEs, code must remain human-readable for now — full 'no-read' development may be 2 to 10 years away and will arrive in risk-based stages.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Senior engineering talent retains value; readability/understandability tooling stays relevant for high-risk domains like banking.
insights.quote: I don't think we're at a point yet where we can 100% trust what's generated.
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: I've had a lot of discussions

insights.claim: Patrick Debois says good human engineering practices (TDD, up-to-date docs, a single code standard) directly improve agent output, and that formal verification is making a comeback as teams specify intent and have agents prove correctness, including via recorded videos of workflows.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Formal-verification and spec-driven tooling could see renewed demand as an AI-code assurance layer.
insights.quote: Formal verification is making a comeback
insights.locator: Formal verification is making a comeback

insights.claim: Patrick Debois constrains agents with two hook-enforced nudges: files may not exceed 200 lines and test coverage must reach 99%, verified by a coverage tool in a hook.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Concrete, cheap guardrails using existing tooling — the opportunity is in enforcement hooks rather than new test frameworks.
insights.quote: One is I say files can't be bigger than 200 lines
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: I do two very small things

insights.claim: Gunnar Grosch reports no change in testing frameworks, but agents have exploded test counts so services that once had few tests now have hundreds, while Renato Losio warns the flood of AI-generated tests adds a lot of noise.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: Test volume is no longer a quality proxy; test-suite curation/flake reduction becomes a cost and CI-compute issue.
insights.quote: The test coverage looks very different with the help of agents.
insights.locator: Gunnar Grosch: I'm not using anything that's specific

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai's organization builds a semantic layer and a forensic layer into its agent harness and uses circuit breakers that force human review when agents write very large amounts of code, because AI handles large context windows poorly.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Enterprise harnesses with circuit breakers are the governance pattern to watch; large-context weakness persists as a limiting factor.
insights.quote: AI has been notoriously poor in handling those kinds of large context windows
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: What my experience goes is

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai says the definition of done is expanding to include checkpoints on correctness, quality, semantics and long-term maintainability, and future human reviewers will focus on whether a system (e.g. 20 microservices) remains maintainable over the long run.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Reviewer role shifts toward architecture/maintainability; maintenance cost of AI code is a key risk to track.
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: One thing which I think is changing

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds argues old delivery principles still hold under AI: a large failed change has the same blast radius whether AI is used or not, so small incremental steps remain the way to limit impact.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Continuous delivery disciplines are reinforced, not obsoleted, by AI — positive for CD platform vendors.
insights.quote: Just because we have AI doesn't mean that we should just throw them out the window.
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: I think that's really interesting

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds says governance matters more on the AI delivery side than the coding side, because coding agents live on a developer machine without production access, whereas agents deploying software and creating infrastructure need new regulated-environment guardrails.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Production-agent governance (policies, approvals, audit) is a higher-value control market than IDE assistant governance.
insights.quote: I think this might sound weird, but it's more important on the delivery side than it is on the coding side.
insights.locator: Martin Reynolds: Introducing AI is no different

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds and Gunnar Grosch argue zero-trust for agents comes down to least privilege: scoped, time-limited credentials tied to a specific agent and pipeline, plus a full audit trail and sandboxing where appropriate — and unlike humans, agents cannot be trusted on good intentions.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: Identity/secrets vendors serving non-human (agent) identities and ephemeral credentials stand to benefit.
insights.quote: They will do what they need to do and they will do what they're allowed to do.
insights.locator: Deterministic Controls/Metrics, for AI, in a Zero-Trust Environment

insights.claim: Patrick Debois argues an AI gateway is needed for control, citing a Claude setup-token command that issued a token valid for a year with no way to revoke it from the console, and the hassle of exposing GitHub personal access tokens to agents.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: AI gateway / token-governance products address a real gap in current agent vendor tooling.
insights.quote: Then before I realized it, this was a token that was a year valid.
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: I think this is also where you really need an AI gateway

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai warns regulated sectors face high shadow-AI risk when central governance 'applies the brakes', and her response has been community-led InnerSourcing frameworks offering centralized persona agents that cover about 80% of jobs and that anyone can spin off.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Over-restrictive AI policies drive shadow adoption; internal agent platforms/catalogs are the mitigation enterprises are buying or building.
insights.quote: the velocity trap is real
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: I'll add to some of the points

insights.claim: Gunnar Grosch, formerly at AWS, says regulated industries have largely moved past the early 'we can't use OpenAI, Anthropic or AWS' objection, but many production AI agents today are black boxes whose behavior their owners cannot audit.
insights.speaker: Gunnar Grosch
insights.so_what: Agent observability/auditability is a near-term buying need — positive for observability vendors extending into AI agents.
insights.quote: Many AI agents that I see in production today, they are black boxes.
insights.locator: Gunnar Grosch: Before joining Sinch

insights.claim: Patrick Debois warns that context artifacts such as skills installed from registries can contain scripts and PII and constitute a new supply-chain surface (alongside prompt injection) that enterprises are not yet governing, analogous to vetting third-party libraries and licenses.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: Supply-chain security vendors have an expansion vector into agent context/skills vetting.
insights.quote: There's a new piece that a lot of enterprises might not be thinking about as this new piece that they need to control as well.
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: The reason, Martin, why I was shaking my head

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai says agents remain heterogeneous with only partial standardization (e.g. MCP) and expects industry work toward interoperable agent ecosystems over the next one to two years.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Interoperability standards could commoditize agent integrations; watch standards-body momentum.
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: One more thing which is very interesting

themes.theme: Economics, open source strain and ROI

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai flags FinOps for token economics as a major enterprise concern, noting that in a 20,000-developer ecosystem token spend becomes a very substantial share of capability.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: AI token spend is becoming a material line item; FinOps/AI cost-governance tooling has demand.
insights.quote: FinOps, how to adopt token economics at scale
insights.locator: The third part, which also from an enterprise perspective

insights.claim: A cited study of 800-plus open-source projects found AI adoption produced only a brief velocity increase before reverting to the median after a few months; Martin Reynolds attributes this to unchanged reviewer capacity, lack of enterprise review tooling and increased caution about injected vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains can be transient without downstream capacity; be skeptical of early velocity claims.
insights.locator: Improving and Sustaining Productivity, with AI

insights.claim: Patrick Debois reports some open-source maintainers no longer accept code changes, instead asking contributors for intent and having their own agents implement it, while tainting externally sourced tickets because they can steer agents.
insights.speaker: Patrick Debois
insights.so_what: The open-source contribution model is shifting from code to intent; untrusted-input tainting is an emerging agent-security requirement.
insights.quote: They ask people for their intent change and they have their agent code that intent.
insights.locator: Patrick Debois: The trend there is

insights.claim: Martin Reynolds says early AI demand was largely FOMO, a huge percentage of started projects were abandoned for lack of discernible outcomes, and buyers are now working backward from measurable outcomes and ROI.
insights.speaker: Martin Reynolds
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI buying is maturing toward outcome-based justification — favors vendors with measurable ROI, pressures 'shiny tool' plays.
insights.quote: A huge percentage of the projects that were started were abandoned.
insights.locator: AI Demand - Use Case Driven vs. FOMO

insights.claim: Garima Bajpai argues the question has moved from FOMO to competitive advantage because a 200-person startup can now replace a 20,000-person enterprise through AI-driven velocity, pushing incumbents toward time-to-market compression and hyper-personalization, with jobs and roles changing.
insights.speaker: Garima Bajpai
insights.so_what: Incumbent disruption risk rises; watch large-enterprise headcount and restructuring tied to AI.
insights.quote: a startup with 200 people can replace a big enterprise with 20,000 people
insights.locator: Garima Bajpai: I want to add here
